pos: n. (the Norwegian Cistercian abbey of 1146 near Bergen, the first of the order in Norway, settled from Fountains)
biblical_def: Lyse south of Bergen was founded in 1146 by Bishop Sigurd of Bergen and settled from Fountains in Yorkshire, the first Cistercian house in Norway and the mother of Tautra and of Hovedoya. Monks came north by sea from an English dale to a Norwegian fjord, cleared and farmed, and the house held estates along the western coast until the Reformation dissolved it in 1537. Little stands. The dictionary records Lyse for the direction of travel, which is the ordinary pattern of Christian expansion: men sent from a settled place to an unsettled one. The Lord's own statement of the problem is a shortage of workers rather than of ground, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and He forbids the delay that always sounds prudent, “Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest” (Joh 4:35). The sowing is expected to cost those who do it, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5), and the charge over whatever congregation results is given in terms of its price, “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending, also a station of missionaries; a fjord would be an inlet of the sea; to colonize as to plant a colony; a daughter-house is a convent founded from another; and harvest as the season of reaping.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending or being sent, usually by authority, on some business; persons sent; a station of missionaries.
FIRTH, n. A narrow arm or inlet of the sea; an estuary; the opening of a river into the sea.
COLONIZE, v.t. To plant or establish a colony in; to plant or settle a number of the subjects of a kingdom in a remote country.
FILIATION, n. The relation of a son to a father; also, the relation of a dependent house to its parent.
HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering grain or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected.
scriptures: Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Joh 4:35
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: Norway's first Cistercian house, 1146, settled from Fountains in Yorkshire, mother of Tautra and Hovedoya.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that expansion is men sent, not territory acquired. Lyse was planted by Yorkshire monks who went north by sea, and the Lord's own account of what is scarce in such work is not land, “but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37).

The live temptation is to count estates instead of converts, which is what the Norwegian houses eventually did. Christ refuses the postponement that makes such counting restful, “Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest?” (Joh 4:35); the sowing is expected to be costly, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5); and the flock that results is valued by what it cost its owner, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28).

pos: n. (the Norwegian Cistercian abbey of 1207 on an island in the Trondheimsfjord, famous for its orchard)
etymology: Old Norse Tautra, from tautr and ey, perhaps the sheltered island.
biblical_def: Tautra is a low island in the Trondheimsfjord, and in 1207 Cistercians from Lyse founded a house there dedicated to the Virgin. It is far north, past the sixty-third parallel, and the monks nonetheless planted an orchard that became locally famous, taking advantage of the fjord's mild water and the island's shelter to grow fruit where the surrounding country could not. The abbey was dissolved in 1537 and the church stands as a ruin; in 1999 a community of Cistercian women settled on the island again. The dictionary records Tautra for that orchard, because fruit in an unlikely latitude is a figure Scripture uses deliberately. The tree the prophet describes is marked by what it is near rather than by its climate, “For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river” (Jer 17:8), and the psalmist's blessed man is planted by another's hand, “And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water” (Psa 1:3). The decisive dependence is stated without qualification, “for without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5), and the prophet's question to those who labour for the wrong crop is pointed, “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an orchard as an inclosure for fruit trees; to graft as to insert a shoot into another stock; latitude as distance from the equator; an island as a tract of land surrounded by water; and fruit as the produce of a tree.
webster_full: ORCHARD, n. An inclosure devoted to the culture of fruit trees; in America, chiefly of apple trees.
GRAFT, v.t. To insert a shoot or scion of one tree or plant into another for propagation.
LATITUDE, n. In geography, the distance of any place from the equator, north or south.
ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded by water.
FRUIT, n. Whatever the earth produces for the nourishment of animals; the produce of a tree or plant.
scriptures: Jer 17:8

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
Psa 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
corruption_summary: Norwegian Cistercian house of 1207 on a Trondheimsfjord island, famous for an orchard grown past the sixty-third parallel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fruitfulness is a matter of what a tree is planted beside. Tautra's monks grew apples north of the sixty-third parallel, and the prophet's figure makes nearness to water the decisive fact rather than the weather, “but her leaf shall be green” (Jer 17:8).

The live temptation is to credit the horticulture. The psalmist keeps the tree passive at the decisive point, “that bringeth forth his fruit in his season” (Psa 1:3); the Lord states the dependence in terms that leave no room for technique, “I am the vine, ye are the branches” (Joh 15:5); and the prophet puts the hard question about effort spent on the wrong harvest, “and your labour for that which satisfieth not?” (Isa 55:2).

pos: n. (the Norwegian Cistercian abbey of 1147 on an island in the Oslofjord, now a ruin inside the city of Oslo)
etymology: Norwegian Hovedoya, the head island, from hoved and oya, an island.
biblical_def: Hovedoya is an island in the Oslofjord, and in 1147 Cistercians from Kirkstead in Lincolnshire founded an abbey there dedicated to the Virgin and St Edmund. It held property across eastern Norway, quarrelled with the city over fishing rights, and was burned and suppressed in 1532, five years before the Reformation reached Norway formally, when the commander of Akershus sacked it. The stones were carried off to build fortifications. The ruins were excavated in the nineteenth century and now sit in a public park, ten minutes by ferry from the centre of Oslo. The dictionary records Hovedoya for the oddity of a monastic ruin inside a modern capital, and for the way Scripture handles such sights. Jeremiah quoted an earlier prophet to the effect that even the temple mount would be farmland, “Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps” (Jer 26:18). The lament over an emptied sanctuary is grief and not commentary, “The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts” (Lam 1:4), and the psalmist reports a sacking as an outrage, “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7). The promise held out to the places themselves is labour, “And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places” (Isa 58:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ruin as the remains of a decayed building; to excavate as to hollow out; a park as a piece of ground inclosed; to sack as to plunder a town; and a precinct as a boundary or limit.
webster_full: RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work.
EXCAVATE, v.t. To hollow; to cut, scoop, dig or wear out the inner part of any thing.
PARK, n. A large piece of ground inclosed and privileged for wild beasts of chase; a pleasure-ground.
SACK, v.t. To storm; to take by storm and plunder; as, to sack a city.
PRECINCT, n. The limit, bound or exterior line encompassing a place; a territorial district.
scriptures: Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and spake to all the people of Judah, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest.
Lam 1:4
The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is in bitterness.
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
corruption_summary: Norwegian Cistercian house of 1147 on an Oslofjord island, sacked in 1532 and now an excavated ruin in a city park.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that ruined sanctuaries are within the ways of God and are still a grief. Hovedoya's stones went into a fortress and its site is now a picnic ground, and Jeremiah had quoted Micah to the effect that even Zion would be ploughed, “and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest” (Jer 26:18).

The live temptation is the park: a ruin becomes scenery and the loss stops registering. Lamentations keeps the register at grief, “her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted” (Lam 1:4); the psalmist reports the burning as an outrage rather than an episode, “the dwelling place of thy name to the ground” (Psa 74:7); and the word spoken over such sites proposes work and not tourism, “thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12).

pos: n. (the Danish Cistercian abbey of 1161 founded by Absalon, afterwards the Soro Academy)
etymology: Danish Soro, the lake island, from so, a lake, and o, an island.
biblical_def: Sorø in Zealand was made a Cistercian house in 1161 by Bishop Absalon of Roskilde, settled from Esrum, and Absalon himself is buried in front of the high altar along with Valdemar IV and other Danish kings. The abbey was dissolved in 1580 and the buildings turned into a school. In 1747 the writer Ludvig Holberg, having no heir, left his whole estate to it on condition that it be reopened as an academy, and Sorø Academy has been one of the principal Danish schools ever since, in the abbey's own buildings beside the lake. The dictionary records Sorø for Holberg's bequest, because a man leaving his property to teach other men's children is the proverb at work, “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children” (Pro 13:22). What a school is for is stated by the psalmist as a transfer across generations, “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). The standard laid on those who teach is a cut made straight, “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15), and the verdict such a steward hopes for names fidelity, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an academy as a school of the higher order; a bequest as something left by will; an heir as one who inherits; an endowment as a permanent provision; and a legacy as a gift by will.
webster_full: ACADEMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.
BEQUEST, n. Something left by will; a legacy.
HEIR, n. The man who succeeds or is to succeed another in the possession of lands, tenements or hereditaments.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution.
LEGACY, n. A bequest; a particular thing given by last will or testament.
scriptures: A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: Danish Cistercian abbey of 1161 founded by Absalon, dissolved 1580, reopened in 1747 as Soro Academy on Holberg's bequest.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an estate left to teach other people's children is the proverb in action. Holberg had no heir and gave everything to a school in a dissolved abbey, and Scripture treats such a bequest as the mark of a good man, “A good man leaveth an inheritance” (Pro 13:22).

The live temptation for an endowed school is to outlive the reason it was endowed, keeping the buildings and the fees and losing the transfer. The psalmist states the purpose as a handing across generations, “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4); the standard on the teachers is exactness with a text, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15); and the commendation at the end is for fidelity rather than endowment, “thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21).

pos: n. (the Lazio Cistercian abbey of 1135, the first of the order in Italy, where Thomas Aquinas died in 1274)
etymology: Italian Fossanova, the new ditch, from fossa, a trench, for the drainage cut there.
biblical_def: Fossanova in southern Lazio was a Benedictine house given to the Cistercians in 1135, the first of the order in Italy, and its name records the drainage cut the monks made through the Pontine marshes. Its church, consecrated in 1208, is the earliest Gothic building in Italy and the model for Cistercian architecture in the peninsula. In March 1274 Thomas Aquinas, travelling to the Council of Lyon, fell ill nearby and died in the abbey's guest quarters. The dictionary records Fossanova for that death, and engages Aquinas as the Reformers did, with respect and without deference. His defence of the Trinity and of the incarnation is the common inheritance of the whole church; his account of grace is far better than the late medieval practice built on it. But a theology that makes philosophy a co-foundation invites the apostolic caution, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8), and the foundation is not a composite, “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). The proverb forbids resting the weight on one's own reasoning, “lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5), and the final court is a written one, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scholastic as pertaining to the schools, also pedantic; philosophy as the knowledge of causes, a system of principles; a summa would be a compendium; reason as the faculty of deducing inferences; and a doctor as a learned man, a teacher.
webster_full: SCHOLASTIC, adj. Pertaining to a scholar, to a school or to schools; pertaining to the schoolmen; pedantic.
PHILOSOPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of the causes of all phenomena, both of mind and of matter.
COMPENDIUM, n. A brief compilation or composition, containing the principal heads or general principles of a larger work.
REASON, n. That intellectual power which deduces inferences from premises; the faculty of rational beings.
DOCTOR, n. A teacher; one versed in any science; a learned man; one who has passed the degrees of a university.
scriptures: Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Italy's first Cistercian house, 1135, with the earliest Gothic church in the peninsula, where Thomas Aquinas died in 1274.
corruption_paragraphs: Aquinas died in a guest room at Fossanova, and the dictionary engages him rather than dismissing him. On the Trinity, on the two natures of Christ, on the reality of God's simplicity he defends what the whole church confesses, and the Reformers read him closely and quoted him often. The objection is to method and to what was later built on it: a theology in which philosophy carries part of the load invites the apostolic warning directly, “after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8).

The corruption is sharper in the system that grew from him than in the man. Trent made his framework the scaffolding for infused righteousness, merit and a sacramental treasury, and the apostolic sentence about footings allows no composite, “can no man lay than that is laid” (1Co 3:11). The proverb forbids resting the weight where the schoolmen rested it, “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart” (Pro 3:5), and the court of final appeal is written and open to any reader, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (the Lazio Cistercian abbey of 1151, a Trappist house keeping one of the great Cistercian Gothic churches of Italy)
etymology: Latin Casa Marii, the house of Marius, for the Roman consul said to have been born nearby.
biblical_def: Casamari in Lazio was founded as a Benedictine house in 1035 and passed to the Cistercians in 1151, taking its name from a tradition that Gaius Marius was born on the spot. Its church and cloister, built between 1203 and 1217, are among the purest Cistercian Gothic buildings in Italy: no tower, no sculpture on the capitals, light admitted through plain openings. The abbey has had a printing house and a library since the eighteenth century and is today a Trappist community, which keeps the strict observance of silence. The dictionary records Casamari for that silence, which the Trappists hold more rigorously than any other order and which Scripture grounds in a presence rather than in a discipline, “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). The desire such a house exists to express is stated by the psalmist as a single request, “One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after” (Psa 27:4), and the affection behind it is confessed plainly, “LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house” (Psa 26:8). The waiting itself is pronounced good, “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Trappist would be a monk of La Trappe; silence as absence of sound, also forbearance of speech; austerity as severity of manners; a capital as the uppermost part of a column; and observance as the keeping of a rule.
webster_full: SILENCE, n. Stillness, or entire absence of sound or noise; also, forbearance of speech in man.
AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
CAPITAL, n. In architecture, the uppermost part of a column or pillar, serving as the head or crowning.
OBSERVANCE, n. The act of observing; performance; respect; the keeping of a rule or custom.
ABSTINENCE, n. In general, the act or practice of voluntarily refraining from any action; a restraint upon the appetites.
scriptures: Hab 2:20
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
Psa 27:4
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.
Psa 26:8
LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth.
Lam 3:26
It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Lazio Cistercian abbey of 1151, a pure Gothic church of 1203, today a Trappist house of the strict observance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that silence is attention to someone rather than a technique on oneself. Casamari's Trappists keep the strictest observance of any order, and the prophet grounds the hush in a presence and a place, “But the LORD is in his holy temple” (Hab 2:20).

The live temptation is the austerity that becomes its own credential, which is the particular danger of a strict observance. Scripture gives the desire a single object rather than a regimen, “to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple” (Psa 27:4); the affection is confessed and not performed, “and the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8); and the waiting is commended as good in itself, “and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).

pos: n. (the Tuscan Cistercian abbey of 1218, a roofless ruin beside the chapel holding a sword set in stone)
etymology: Italian San Galgano, for Galgano Guidotti, the knight of the founding legend.
biblical_def: San Galgano in the Sienese hills was founded in 1218 beside the hermitage of Montesiepi, where Galgano Guidotti, a knight said to have been converted from a violent life about 1180, is reported to have thrust his sword into a rock to make a cross and lived out his days as a hermit. A sword fixed in stone is still shown there. The abbey became wealthy, supplied Siena with its city treasurers, and then decayed; the roof and campanile fell in the eighteenth century, and the great Gothic church stands open to the sky, one of the most photographed ruins in Italy. The dictionary records San Galgano for the sword, because a legend that supplies its own relic is the mechanism of corruption in miniature. Paul feared precisely this kind of displacement for a congregation, “so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3), and named the apparatus by which it happens, “after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world” (Col 2:8). Christ quoted Isaiah against worship furnished by men, “in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mar 7:7), and the test that would have stopped the sword before it was venerated is written, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hermit as a solitary; a legend as a chronicle of saints, also an idle story; a relic as what is kept with veneration; a campanile would be a bell tower; and simplicity as plainness, freedom from artifice.
webster_full: HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret.
LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints; any memorial or relation; an idle or ridiculous story.
RELIC, n. The remains of a dead body; also, that which is kept in remembrance with veneration.
BELFRY, n. That part of a steeple or other building, in which a bell is hung.
SIMPLICITY, n. Plainness; artlessness; freedom from artifice, duplicity or guile.
scriptures: But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Mar 7:7
Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Tuscan Cistercian abbey of 1218, now a roofless ruin, beside a chapel showing a sword fixed in stone.
corruption_paragraphs: A knight's conversion is a good story and may well be a true one. What happened to it at Montesiepi is the pattern of corruption in small: the story produced an object, the object produced pilgrims, and the pilgrims produced an income. Paul feared exactly this drift for a congregation he had taught himself, “But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty” (2Co 11:3).

The corruption is not peculiar to swords or to Tuscany. Any devotion that grows from a narrative nobody can test runs on the same machinery, and Paul names the parts, “Beware lest any man spoil you” (Col 2:8). Christ's quotation of Isaiah is the verdict on worship furnished out of human invention, “Howbeit in vain do they worship me” (Mar 7:7), and the test that would have stopped the whole business at the start is available to any reader, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

Greek haplotes (G0572) — simplicity, singleness of heart; “the simplicity that is in Christ”, 2 Corinthians 11:3.
Greek sulagogeo (G4812) — to carry off as spoil; “lest any man spoil you”, Colossians 2:8.
Greek entalma (G1778) — a commandment, an injunction of men; “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men”, Mark 7:7.

pos: n. (the Ligurian Cistercian abbey of 1120, the first house of the order founded outside France)
etymology: Italian Tiglieto, the lime grove, from tiglio, a lime tree.
biblical_def: Tiglieto in the Ligurian Apennines was founded in 1120 from Le Thoronet's mother house at La Ferté, and it is the first Cistercian abbey established anywhere outside France, nineteen years before the order reached England by its own reckoning and long before it reached the north. It was a poor house in difficult hill country, it founded Staffarda and other Piedmontese daughters, and after centuries as a private estate a small Cistercian community returned in 2000. The dictionary records Tiglieto as the first step of a very long journey, and for the figure Scripture gives to such journeys. The image is a race run among witnesses, with patience as the required quality rather than speed, “let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1), and Paul keeps the figure while insisting on a purpose, “So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24). The shortage in any such work is of workers and not of ground, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and the cost of the sowing is stated at the outset, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a race as a contest in running; a prize as a reward offered; patience as endurance of affliction with calmness; a lime-tree as the linden; and primogeniture as the state of being first-born.
webster_full: RACE, n. A running; a rapid course or motion; a contest in running; competition.
PRIZE, n. A reward gained by contest with competitors; that which is won.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance.
LINDEN, n. The lime-tree, a tree of the genus Tilia.
PRIMOGENITURE, n. The state of being first-born; seniority by birth among children.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
corruption_summary: The first Cistercian abbey founded outside France, 1120, in the Ligurian Apennines, mother of Staffarda.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a long expansion begins with one poor house in bad country. Tiglieto was the order's first foundation outside France, and the figure Scripture gives such an undertaking puts the stress on endurance, “so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1).

The live temptation is to confuse being first with having arrived. Paul attaches a purpose to the running so that the race is not its own reward, “but one receiveth the prize?” (1Co 9:24); the Lord names what is actually in short supply, “but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37); and the cost is declared at the start rather than discovered later, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5).
roots_summary: Greek hupomone (G5281), patient endurance; Greek brabeion (G1017), a prize; Greek ergates (G2040), a workman; Hebrew zara (H2232), to sow.
roots_lines: Greek hupomone (G5281) — patient endurance, steadfastness; “let us run with patience”, Hebrews 12:1.
Greek agon (G0073) — a contest, a race, a struggle; “the race that is set before us”, Hebrews 12:1.
Greek brabeion (G1017) — a prize awarded in the games; “but one receiveth the prize?”, 1 Corinthians 9:24.
Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a labourer; “but the labourers are few”, Matthew 9:37.
Hebrew zara (H2232) — to sow, to scatter seed; “They that sow in tears”, Psalm 126:5.
usage: “let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1) — the stress on endurance.
“So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24) — a purpose attached to the running.
“but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — what is in short supply.

pos: n. (the Piedmontese Cistercian abbey of 1135, keeping a medieval market hall, beside the battlefield of 1690)
etymology: Italian Staffarda, of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Lombard personal name.
biblical_def: Staffarda in Piedmont was founded in 1135 on marshland given by the marquis of Saluzzo and settled from Tiglieto. The monks drained the plain and the abbey grew rich on grain and cattle, and it kept something few monasteries kept: a covered market hall of the fifteenth century in the abbey precinct, where its tenants and neighbours traded under the abbey's measures and paid the abbey's dues. In 1690 the French under Catinat beat the Savoyard army on the fields beside it and sacked the buildings. The dictionary records Staffarda for that market, because a monastery that owned the scales is the clearest case of the order's commercial turn. Scripture does not condemn trade; it questions what it buys, “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2), and it promises honest labour a return, “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23). The requirement laid on whoever holds the measures is a single one, “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2), and the Lord's warning to a prospering house concerns an arithmetic rather than an income, “a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a market as a public place where provisions are exposed for sale; a measure as that by which extent or quantity is ascertained; toll as a tax for a privilege; a tenant as one who holds lands of another; and traffick as commerce, trade.
webster_full: MARKET, n. A public place in a city or town, where provisions or cattle are exposed for sale; a public building in which provisions are sold.
MEASURE, n. The whole extent or dimensions of a thing; that by which extent or dimension is ascertained.
TOLL, n. A tax paid for some liberty or privilege, particularly for passage over a bridge or on a highway.
TENANT, n. One who holds or possesses lands or tenements by any kind of right or title.
TRAFFICK, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling.
scriptures: Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
corruption_summary: Piedmontese Cistercian abbey of 1135 with a fifteenth-century market hall in its precinct, sacked after the battle of 1690.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that owning the scales is a trust and not merely an advantage. Staffarda's tenants traded under the abbey's measures in the abbey's hall, and the prophet's question to any market is about what the money buys, “hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good” (Isa 55:2).

The live temptation is the one the Cistercians took: a house founded on austerity ends up holding the weights. The proverb grants honest work its return without apology, “but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23); the requirement on a man handling what is not his own is single, “that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2); and the Lord forbids the arithmetic that equates life with holdings, “Take heed, and beware of covetousness” (Luk 12:15).
roots_summary: Hebrew sabea (H7646), to be satisfied; Hebrew mothar (H4195), profit; Greek oikonomos (G3623), a steward; Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness.

Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward, a house-manager; “it is required in stewards”, 1 Corinthians 4:2.

“that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2) — the requirement on whoever holds the scales.
“Take heed, and beware of covetousness” (Luk 12:15) — the arithmetic forbidden.

pos: n. (the Calabrian Cistercian abbey of about 1160, where Joachim of Fiore was a monk before founding his own order)
etymology: Italian Sambucina, the elder grove, from sambuco, an elder tree.
biblical_def: Sambucina in Calabria was founded about 1160 from Casamari and became the chief Cistercian house of the far south, mother of several Calabrian and Sicilian daughters. Its most consequential member passed through rather than stayed: Joachim of Fiore, who was a monk and for a time abbot in the Calabrian Cistercian houses before withdrawing to found his own congregation at San Giovanni in Fiore about 1196. Joachim divided history into three ages, of the Father, the Son and the Spirit, and taught that a third age of spiritual understanding was about to begin around 1260. The dictionary records Sambucina for that scheme, which has been the template of every later claim that the church has entered a new dispensation of the Spirit. The faith was delivered once and is not succeeded, “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and no later messenger is exempt from the test, “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you” (Gal 1:8). Paul names the apparatus out of which such systems are assembled, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8), and describes exactly what a congregation forfeits when it takes one up, “so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3). Joachim was by all accounts a devout man, and the dictionary says so; his scheme is still the seed of every announcement that the written word has been overtaken.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a millenarian as one who believes in the millennium; chiliasm would be the doctrine of a thousand years; a dispensation as the dealing of God with his creatures, also a system; prophecy as a foretelling; and speculation as mental view of a subject, a theory.
webster_full: MILLENARIAN, n. One who believes in the millennium, and that it will commence at a particular time.
DISPENSATION, n. The dealing of God to his creatures; the distribution of good and evil, natural or moral, in the divine government.
PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come, which human sagacity could not foresee.
SPECULATION, n. Mental view of any thing in its various aspects and relations; a train of thoughts formed by meditation; a theory.
ADVENT, n. A coming; appropriately the coming of our Savior; a season of devotion before Christmas.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
corruption_summary: Calabria's chief Cistercian house of about 1160, where Joachim of Fiore was a monk before founding his own congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: Joachim of Fiore learned his monasticism in the Calabrian Cistercian houses and then left them to teach a scheme of three ages: the Father's, the Son's, and a coming age of the Spirit in which the institutional church and even the letter of the Gospel would be superseded by spiritual understanding. It has been the master template ever since for every announcement that the church has entered a new dispensation. Scripture forecloses it, “it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you” (Jud 1:3).

The pattern is alive. Dispensational schemes that carve history into ages with different terms of acceptance, and modern apostolic-and-prophetic movements that claim a fresh outpouring superseding the written word, both work Joachim's ground. The apostolic test admits no exemption for the messenger, “than that which we have preached unto you” (Gal 1:8); Paul names the apparatus such systems are built from, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8); and he describes what a congregation loses when it accepts one, “so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3).
